t.1.1.2: As the gifts were being led away, faith entered into him, though he was only a boy. He thought:
t.1.1.1: Desiring the reward of his sacrifice, the son of Vājaśravas gave away all that he owned. He had a son named Naciketas.
t.1.1.4: He said to his father, "Father, to whom will you give me?" He asked a second time, and a third. To him the father said, "To Death I give you."
t.1.1.3: Those that have drunk their last water, eaten their last grass, yielded their last milk, and lost their strength: joyless indeed are the worlds to which he goes who gives such things.
t.1.1.5: Among many I go as the first, among many I go as the middle; what, I wonder, is the task of Yama that he will accomplish through me today?
t.1.1.6: Look back and see how those who came before fared; look around and see how it is with those who come after. Like grain a mortal ripens, and like grain he is born again.
t.1.1.7: A Brāhmaṇa guest enters houses like Vaiśvānara, the fire. For him they perform this appeasement: bring water, O Vaivasvata!
t.1.1.9: Since you, O Brahmin, a guest worthy of reverence, have dwelt in my house for three nights without eating, let there be salutation to you, O Brahmin, and may there be well-being for me; therefore choose three boons in return.
t.1.1.8: Hope and expectation, fellowship and kindly speech, all that he has gained in sacrifices and pious works, his sons and cattle, every one of them: all this a brāhmaṇa wrests from the man of little understanding in whose house he stays without eating.
t.1.1.10: O Mṛtyu, that Gautama may be calmed in his intent, kindly in mind, and free of anger toward me, and that he may recognize me and greet me when I am sent back by you: this I choose as the first of the three boons.
t.1.1.11: As before, Auddālaki Āruṇi, released by me, will recognize you and be well-disposed toward you; his anger gone, he will sleep peacefully through the nights, having seen you freed from the mouth of death.
t.1.1.12: In the heavenly world there is no fear at all; you are not there, and no one fears old age. Having crossed beyond both hunger and thirst, and passing beyond sorrow, one rejoices in the heavenly world.
t.1.1.13: You, O Mṛtyu, know the fire that leads to heaven; explain it to me, for I have faith. Those who dwell in the heavenly worlds enjoy immortality; this I choose as my second boon.
t.1.1.15: He told him of that fire which is the beginning of the worlds: what bricks are used, how many, and in what way they are laid. And he repeated it back just as it had been told; then Mṛtyu, pleased with him, spoke again.
t.1.1.14: Knowing it well, I shall declare to you the fire that leads to heaven, O Naciketas; learn it from me. Know this fire to be the attainment of endless worlds and their foundation, hidden in the secret place.
t.1.1.16: Delighted, the great-souled one said to him: "I give you here today yet another boon: this fire shall be known by your very name. And take this chain of many forms."
t.1.1.17: He who has kindled the Nāciketa fire three times, having gained union with the three and performed the three duties, crosses beyond birth and death. Knowing the omniscient one born of Brahman, the god worthy of praise, and realizing him, he attains this peace forever.
t.1.1.18: He who has thrice performed the Nāciketa fire, having known this triad, and who, knowing thus, builds up the Nāciketa fire, casts off the fetters of death before him and, passing beyond sorrow, rejoices in the world of heaven.
t.1.1.19: This, O Naciketas, is your fire that leads to heaven, which you chose as your second boon; this fire people will call by your name alone. Choose now, O Naciketas, your third boon.
t.1.1.20: There is this doubt concerning a man who has departed: some say, "He exists," and some say, "He does not exist." Instructed by you, I would know this; of the boons, this is the third boon.
t.1.1.21: Even the gods of old had doubt about this, for it is not easy to understand; subtle is this matter. Choose another boon, Naciketas; do not press me, release me from this.
t.1.1.23: Choose sons and grandsons who will live a hundred years, many cattle, elephants and gold, and horses; choose a vast domain of the earth, and live yourself for as many autumns as you wish.
t.1.1.24: If you think any boon equal to this, choose it: wealth and long life. Be great on the wide earth, Naciketas; I will make you an enjoyer of all desires.
t.1.1.22: Even the gods, it is said, had doubt about this, and you yourself, O Mṛtyu, say that it is not easy to know. No other like you who will speak of it can be found, and no other boon is equal to this one.
t.1.1.25: Whatever desires are hard to obtain in the world of mortals, ask for all those desires as you wish; here are these lovely maidens with chariots and with musical instruments, for such as these are not to be won by men. Be waited upon by these, given by me, O Naciketas, but do not ask about death.
t.1.1.26: Ephemeral are these things, O Antaka, for they wear away the vigour of all the senses of a mortal. Even an entire life is brief indeed; yours alone be the horses, yours the dancing and the songs.
t.1.1.27: Not by wealth can a man be satisfied; we shall obtain wealth if we have but seen you, and we shall live as long as you hold sway. But the boon to be chosen by me is that alone.
t.1.1.28: Having come near the agelessness of the immortals, what aging mortal dwelling on the earth below, knowing this and reflecting on the delights of beauty and love, would take pleasure in an overlong life?
t.1.1.29: That about which men are in doubt, O Death, that which concerns the great passing beyond, tell us that. This boon, which has entered into the hidden mystery, Naciketas chooses no other boon than that.
